serengeti.summary: Endless plains, big cats and the Great Migration.
serengeti.description:
The Serengeti is Tanzania's best-known park, a vast ecosystem of open grassland, kopjes (granite outcrops) and river woodland that stretches north towards Kenya's Maasai Mara. It is home to lion, leopard, cheetah, elephant, giraffe, hippo and enormous herds of plains game, and it is one of the few places where you can reliably find all of the big cats in a single trip.
The park is best known for the wildebeest migration, in which well over a million wildebeest, along with zebra and gazelle, follow the rains in a rough circle through the ecosystem. Calving takes place on the southern plains around Ndutu from roughly December to March. The herds move through the central and western Serengeti in the middle of the year, and the dramatic Mara River crossings in the north usually happen between about July and October. Exact timing changes from year to year, so a good itinerary stays flexible.
Good to know: the Serengeti is large, so most visitors spend two to three nights to see more than one area. Game drives start early and finish late, and many lodges and camps are small and seasonal. Wildlife is excellent all year, and the best choice of area depends on the month you travel.

ngorongoro-crater.summary: A UNESCO-listed caldera packed with wildlife.
ngorongoro-crater.description:
The Ngorongoro Crater is the world's largest intact volcanic caldera, about 260 square kilometres across, with walls that rise some 600 metres above the floor. Because the crater is so enclosed, wildlife can be found in a small area: lion, hyena, buffalo, elephant, hippo, flamingos on the soda lake and, with luck, the endangered black rhino.
Most visits are a single early-morning descent with a picnic lunch on the crater floor, followed by a climb back to the rim in the afternoon. The rim sits at around 2,300 metres, so evenings are cool and mornings can be misty, and a warm layer is useful even in the dry season. The wider Ngorongoro Conservation Area is a multiple-use area where Maasai pastoralists live alongside wildlife, and it also includes Olduvai Gorge, a key site for the study of early humans.
The crater is busy in peak months, so an early start makes a real difference to the experience. It combines naturally with the Serengeti, Tarangire and Lake Manyara on the Northern Circuit.

tarangire.summary: Elephants, baobabs and dry-season game viewing.
tarangire.description:
Tarangire National Park is known for its big elephant herds and its ancient baobab trees, which dot a landscape of rolling hills, swamps and the permanent Tarangire River. It is one of the best parks in Tanzania for elephants and has a rich bird list, along with lion, leopard, giraffe, zebra, wildebeest and the occasional python seen in the trees.
The park is at its best in the dry season, from about June to October, when animals from the surrounding plains gather along the river and wildlife viewing is concentrated and easy. During the wet months the park turns green and quieter, with excellent birding but wildlife more spread out.
Tarangire is close to Arusha, about two to three hours by road, which makes it a popular first stop on the Northern Circuit and a practical choice for a one-day or two-day trip.

lake-manyara.summary: A compact park of forest, flamingos and tree-climbing lions.
lake-manyara.description:
Lake Manyara National Park lies at the foot of the Rift Valley escarpment and packs a wide variety of habitats into a small area: groundwater forest, acacia woodland, open grassland and the shallow alkaline lake itself. It is a good park for large troops of baboons, blue monkeys, elephants, hippo, giraffe and an exceptional range of birds, including flamingos and pelicans when water levels suit them.
The park is known for tree-climbing lions, although sightings are never guaranteed. The lake changes with the rains, so what you see varies by season, and the park is often combined with Tarangire or Ngorongoro rather than visited on its own. It is a gentle, scenic day or half day that suits families and travellers who want variety rather than big herds.

lake-eyasi.summary: A cultural stop with Hadzabe and Datoga communities.
lake-eyasi.description:
Lake Eyasi is a shallow, seasonal soda lake in the Rift Valley south of the Serengeti, and it is best known as a cultural destination rather than a game park. The area is home to the Hadzabe, one of the last hunter-gatherer communities in Africa, and to Datoga pastoralists and blacksmiths.
Visits are usually arranged with local guides and include a morning hunting walk with Hadzabe hunters, or a visit to a Datoga homestead. These are best approached as respectful, small-group visits, with the community benefiting directly. The area is hot and dry, so an early start and sun protection matter, and the lake level changes a lot between seasons. Lake Eyasi sits naturally between Lake Manyara and Ngorongoro on a longer Northern Circuit itinerary.

lengai-natron.summary: Oldoinyo Lengai volcano and the flamingo-lined Lake Natron.
lengai-natron.description:
Oldoinyo Lengai, the Mountain of God in the Maasai language, is an active volcano in the north of the Rift Valley, and Lake Natron lies just below it. The lake is a shallow, very alkaline soda lake and one of the most important breeding grounds for lesser flamingos in East Africa, set in a stark, dramatic landscape of salt flats, escarpment and waterfalls.
The region is remote and hot, with limited facilities, and offers walking, cultural visits and waterfall hikes. The climb of Oldoinyo Lengai is a steep, demanding overnight ascent that begins around midnight to reach the crater rim before sunrise, so it is suitable only for fit walkers who are comfortable on loose volcanic ground. Conditions at the summit can change, so we plan this with local guides and confirm the route before you go.

mikumi.summary: Easy-access savanna close to Dar es Salaam.
mikumi.description:
Mikumi National Park is one of the most accessible safari parks in Tanzania, within a few hours' drive of Dar es Salaam and with scheduled flights from Zanzibar. Its open floodplain, the Mkata plain, is good for giraffe, zebra, buffalo, wildebeest, elephant and hippo, and lion are seen with some regularity.
Because of its location, Mikumi works well as a short safari from Dar es Salaam or Zanzibar and as a gentle introduction to the southern circuit. It is also easy to combine with the Udzungwa Mountains. It is quieter than the north, with fewer vehicles, although the main road runs along one edge of the park.

nyerere.summary: Boats, walks and the wild south.
nyerere.description:
Nyerere National Park, formerly the northern part of the Selous Game Reserve, is one of the largest protected areas in Africa and is centred on the Rufiji River and its network of lakes and channels. Unlike most Tanzanian parks it allows boat safaris and guided walking safaris, in addition to game drives, so you can see hippo, crocodile and elephants from the water and track wildlife on foot.
Wildlife includes elephant, buffalo, giraffe, lion, wild dog and a very large bird list. The park is remote, usually reached by short scheduled flight, and has few vehicles. It suits travellers who want a quieter safari and an alternative to the Northern Circuit, or a second trip. Some camps close in the wettest months, so dates should be checked when planning.

ruaha.summary: Rugged country and big lion prides.
ruaha.description:
Ruaha National Park is the largest national park in Tanzania, a wild and rugged landscape of baobab-studded hills, open bush and the seasonal Great Ruaha River. It is known for large prides of lion, strong numbers of elephant and buffalo, and a mix of species seen less often further north, such as greater kudu and sable and roan antelope.
The best wildlife viewing is in the dry season, from roughly June to October, when game concentrates along the river. Ruaha is remote and usually reached by a light aircraft, with a small number of camps and very few vehicles, so it appeals to travellers who value space and solitude over a busy schedule.

zanzibar.summary: Stone Town, spice farms and Indian Ocean beaches.
zanzibar.description:
Zanzibar is a tropical island off the Tanzanian coast with white-sand beaches, clear water and a long Swahili and Omani history. Stone Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is a maze of narrow lanes, carved doors, markets and old merchant houses, and it is worth at least a half day on foot with a guide.
Outside Stone Town, you can visit spice farms, swim with dolphins, snorkel on the coral reefs or simply relax on the beach. The north and east coasts have different characters: the north coast, around Nungwi and Kendwa, has deeper water for swimming at all tides, while the east coast has big tidal changes, which affect swimming and water sports. Zanzibar is a natural end to a safari, and the main seasons are the dry months from June to October and January to February.

kilimanjaro.description:
Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa, and the world's tallest free-standing mountain, rising to 5,895 metres at Uhuru Peak. You do not need technical climbing skills to reach the summit, but it is a serious high-altitude trek, and the biggest factor in success is giving your body enough time to acclimatise, which is why longer routes have better summit rates.
There are several routes, each with its own character: Marangu, with huts; Machame and Lemosho, with scenic camps and a gradual profile; Rongai, from the north, which is drier; Umbwe, steep and direct; and the Northern Circuit, the longest route and the best for acclimatisation. The mountain passes through rainforest, moorland, alpine desert and a summit zone of ice and rock, and the weather can change quickly.
The main climbing seasons are January to March and June to October. All climbs must be done with a registered guide, and we provide guides, porters and cooks. Training, good gear and a calm pace matter more than raw fitness.

mount-meru.summary: A rewarding climb and a good Kilimanjaro warm-up.
mount-meru.description:
Mount Meru, at 4,566 metres, is the second-highest mountain in Tanzania and rises above Arusha National Park. The standard route, from Momella Gate, takes in forest, a crater rim and a long, narrow ridge, with a good chance of seeing buffalo, giraffe and monkeys on the lower slopes, which is why an armed ranger accompanies each group.
Meru is a challenging climb in its own right, usually done in three to four days, and it is also a well-regarded acclimatisation trek before Kilimanjaro. The views of Kilimanjaro at sunrise from the crater rim are a highlight.

usambara.summary: Cool mountain villages, forests and viewpoints.
usambara.description:
The Usambara Mountains, in north-eastern Tanzania, are part of the Eastern Arc range and are known for their cool climate, terraced farms, forest reserves and wide views over the plains. The area is excellent for walking between villages, with local guides, and is rich in birdlife and endemic plants.
It suits travellers who want a quiet, cultural walking experience away from the main safari parks, and it is typically reached from Arusha or Tanga. Trails are mostly moderate and can be muddy in the rains, so good footwear is useful.

blog.title: Tanzania safari guide
blog.excerpt: When to go, which parks to choose and how to plan a first Tanzania safari.
blog.body:
Tanzania offers some of the best wildlife viewing in Africa, and planning a first trip is mostly about three choices: when to go, which parks to visit and how long to stay.
When to go. The dry season, from about June to October, is the classic time for a safari: animals gather around water, vegetation is thin and roads are easier. January to March is also excellent in the southern Serengeti, where wildebeest calve around Ndutu. The long rains from roughly April to May are the quietest months, with lower prices and fewer vehicles but more mud and some closed camps. The short rains in November and December are usually brief and can be very good value.
Which parks. The Northern Circuit, which includes Tarangire, Lake Manyara, the Serengeti and the Ngorongoro Crater, is the classic route and works for first-time visitors. The southern parks, such as Nyerere and Ruaha, are quieter, and add boating and walking safaris. Many travellers finish with a few days on Zanzibar.
How long. Four to seven days lets you see more than one park without rushing. If you can, spend at least two nights in the Serengeti, and avoid more than a couple of long drive days back to back.
Budget and style. Prices depend on accommodation level, group size and whether you travel privately or on a shared departure. A joining safari is the most economical, a private mid-range safari gives you control over timing, and a luxury or fly-in safari saves road time. Ask for a clear list of what is included, and what is not, before you compare quotes.
What to pack. Neutral clothing, a warm layer for early mornings, sun protection, binoculars, a camera and any personal medication. Soft bags are easier to load than hard suitcases.

blog.title: Fly-in safaris
blog.excerpt: Bush flights, baggage limits and when flying beats driving.
blog.body:
A fly-in safari replaces long drives between parks with short scheduled or charter flights on light aircraft, landing on airstrips close to the camp. It can turn a long road day into a flight of under an hour.
When it is worth it. Flying makes the most sense when you have limited time, when the park is far from Arusha or Dar es Salaam, or when you want to combine a safari with Zanzibar without returning by road. Remote southern parks such as Ruaha and Nyerere are almost always reached by air. In the Serengeti, a flight can save most of a day each way.
What to expect. Flights are on small aircraft with limited seating, and routes can include several stops. Baggage allowances are strict, usually around 15 kilograms in a soft bag, so pack light and ask what is allowed before you travel. Extra luggage can often be stored at your hotel or the airline's base.
Cost and trade-offs. Flying costs more than driving, but you gain game-viewing time and see the country from above. A mix is common: drive in, fly out, or the reverse. Weather can sometimes delay flights, so a small buffer on the last day is wise.

blog.title: Serengeti balloon safari
blog.excerpt: What to expect on a sunrise balloon flight and how to book it.
blog.body:
A hot-air balloon flight over the Serengeti is one of the most memorable activities in Tanzania. Flights depart at first light from the central Serengeti, usually near Seronera, and drift quietly over the plains for about an hour, followed by a bush breakfast on landing.
What you see. From the air you get a sense of the scale of the landscape, and you may see herds, giraffe, elephants and sometimes predators. The balloon cannot be steered precisely, so the route depends on the wind and wildlife sightings are a bonus rather than a promise.
Booking. Flights run by licensed operators and are limited by the number of baskets, so it is best to reserve early, especially in the migration months. We usually arrange them as an extra on a Serengeti stay. The activity needs an early start, so plan to stay overnight nearby.
Practical notes. Wear warm layers because dawn is cool, and avoid loose hats. The flight can be cancelled for weather, in which case operators normally offer a refund or a different date. Age and health limits apply, so ask when booking.

blog.title: Photographic safari
blog.excerpt: Best parks, months and vehicle set-up for wildlife photography.
blog.body:
A photographic safari focuses on time and positioning rather than distance covered. The aim is fewer moves, longer stays at sightings and a vehicle set up for cameras.
Vehicle set-up. A private vehicle with a window seat for each person is key, ideally with a roof that opens fully, a beanbag or a clamp for long lenses and a power source for charging. Ask the guide to position the vehicle with the light in mind, and to turn the engine off at sightings to reduce vibration.
Best parks and months. The Serengeti offers variety year-round, with river crossings from about July to October and calving on the southern plains around January to March. Ngorongoro Crater gives close, contrasting views, and Tarangire is excellent for elephants in the dry season. Dry-season light is often clearer, while the green season has dramatic skies and fresh foliage.
Gear. A zoom of around 100 to 400 millimetres suits most sightings, with a wide lens for landscapes. Bring spare batteries and cards, a dust cover and a cleaning cloth, since dust is a constant. Shoot in the early morning and late afternoon for the best light and most activity.

blog.title: Camping safari
blog.excerpt: What a camping safari is really like in the bush.
blog.body:
A camping safari keeps costs down and puts you close to the sounds of the bush. On most budget and shared departures you sleep in tents at public or special campsites inside or near the parks, with a cook, a guide and often a support crew.
What is provided. Normally a tent, sleeping mats, meals prepared by a camp cook, drinking water and park fees are included. You may need to bring or rent your own sleeping bag, and a small pillow is a useful comfort. Facilities at public campsites are simple, with shared toilets and cold or limited water.
What it feels like. Nights can be cool, especially at higher places such as the Ngorongoro crater rim, and you will hear lions, hyenas and other animals around the camp. Wildlife can wander through public campsites, so you follow the guide's instructions and keep food secure.
Who it suits. It suits travellers who value value for money and do not mind basic comfort. If privacy, hot showers and a proper bed matter, a lodge or tented camp is a better choice, and a mix is also possible.

blog.title: Nyerere National Park
blog.excerpt: Boats, walks and the wild south of Tanzania.
blog.body:
Nyerere National Park, in southern Tanzania, offers a different safari to the north. The park is built around the Rufiji River and its lakes, so you can explore by boat as well as by vehicle, and many camps offer guided walking safaris with armed rangers.
Wildlife. Expect hippo and crocodile in the river, elephant, buffalo, giraffe and a strong bird list, with lion, wild dog and other predators seen with luck. Seeing animals from a boat or on foot gives a closer, quieter view than a vehicle.
Getting there. Most visitors fly from Dar es Salaam or Zanzibar in under an hour, and some arrive by road or train. It works well as a short add-on at either end of a trip or as a main safari for people who want fewer vehicles.
When to go. The dry season, from June to October, is the best for game, while the wet season brings green scenery and birds but some camps close. Check the dates when planning.

blog.title: Northern vs southern Tanzania safari circuit
blog.excerpt: How the two main safari regions compare, and which suits you.
blog.body:
Tanzania has two main safari regions, and the right one depends on what you want from the trip.
The northern circuit. It includes Tarangire, Lake Manyara, the Serengeti and Ngorongoro Crater. It is the most popular, with the highest chance of seeing the big cats and the wildebeest migration, and it is easy to reach from Arusha. It also has the most vehicles and the widest choice of lodges and camps.
The southern circuit. It covers Nyerere, Ruaha and Mikumi. It is quieter, with fewer vehicles and activities such as boat trips and walking safaris. Distances are long, so most visitors fly, and the camps are fewer and often smaller.
Which to choose. For a first safari or a short trip, the north is usually the easier choice. For a second trip, or if you want solitude, boating and walking, the south is very rewarding. Both can be combined with a beach stay on Zanzibar or the coast.

blog.title: Best Kilimanjaro route compared
blog.excerpt: A plain comparison of Kilimanjaro's main routes.
blog.body:
There is no single best Kilimanjaro route, but there is a best route for your priorities. In general, more days on the mountain means a better chance of reaching the summit, because it gives your body time to adapt.
Lemosho. A scenic, gradual route from the west, usually done over seven or eight days. It has a good acclimatisation profile and fewer crowds at the start, and is often recommended for first-time climbers.
Machame. Popular and scenic, usually six or seven days, with steeper days and more traffic on the trail. It suits fit trekkers who like a varied route.
Marangu. The only route with huts, usually five or six days. It is sometimes seen as easier because of the shelter, but the short schedule gives less time to acclimatise, so many people prefer to add a day.
Rongai. From the north, with a gentler gradient and drier conditions, which suits the rainy months. It is quieter and a good choice if you prefer less rain.
Umbwe. A steep, direct route that suits experienced and well-acclimatised trekkers.
Northern Circuit. The longest route, around nine days, with excellent acclimatisation and quiet trails on the north side.
Whichever route you choose, go slowly, drink plenty of water and listen to your guide.

blog.title: Altitude sickness on Kilimanjaro
blog.excerpt: How to recognise, reduce and respond to altitude sickness.
blog.body:
Altitude sickness can affect anyone on Kilimanjaro, regardless of fitness, because the air has less oxygen at height. The most important protection is to climb slowly, take a route with enough days and follow your guide's advice.
Symptoms. Early signs include headache, nausea, dizziness, loss of appetite and trouble sleeping. These are common and usually mild. Warning signs of serious illness include a severe headache that does not ease, vomiting, loss of balance or coordination, confusion, breathlessness at rest and a persistent wet cough. These need action straight away, and descending is the most effective treatment.
Prevention. Choose a longer route, walk slowly (pole pole in Swahili), drink plenty of fluids, eat even when you are not hungry and avoid alcohol. Some climbers use medication such as acetazolamide. Speak to a doctor with experience of altitude before you travel, as it is not suitable for everyone.
When to turn back. Your guides check oxygen levels and symptoms each day. If they advise you to descend, follow that advice. No summit is worth risking your health.

blog.title: Money and tipping in Tanzania
blog.excerpt: Currency, cards, cash and tipping guidance for safaris and climbs.
blog.body:
The local currency is the Tanzanian shilling, but US dollars are widely used for larger payments on safari. Cards are accepted at many hotels and lodges, often with a fee, but cash is still useful for small purchases, tips and markets.
Cash. Bring clean, undamaged US notes, ideally printed in recent years, as older or marked notes are sometimes refused. Smaller notes are handy for tips. ATMs are available in Arusha, Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar but are not available inside the parks.
Tipping. Tipping is customary and appreciated, and guidance varies by operator, so we explain our suggested amounts before you travel. As a rough guide, guides, cooks and porters are usually tipped per day, either individually or as a group. On Kilimanjaro, tips are often shared among the crew in agreed proportions at the end of the climb.
Plan ahead. Tell your bank you are travelling, carry a spare card and keep cash in more than one place. Ask us about any items not included in your price.

blog.title: Is Tanzania safe for tourists?
blog.excerpt: Honest advice on safety, health and common-sense precautions.
blog.body:
Tanzania is a popular and generally welcoming destination, and most visitors have trouble-free trips. As anywhere, a few sensible precautions help.
In towns. Petty theft, such as bag snatching, can happen in busy areas, so keep valuables out of sight, avoid walking alone at night and use registered taxis or your operator's transfer. Keep copies of your passport.
On safari. Your guide's instructions on wildlife are essential. Stay in the vehicle unless told otherwise, keep a safe distance and never feed animals. Roads can be rough, and a good driver-guide makes a big difference.
Health. See a travel doctor well before your trip about vaccinations, malaria prevention and any personal needs, and carry travel insurance that covers medical evacuation. Use insect repellent, drink bottled or treated water and take sun protection.
Before you go. Check your government's current travel advice, entry rules and any visa requirements, as these change.

faqs.question: When is the best time to go on safari in Tanzania?
faqs.answer: The dry season from about June to October is the classic time for wildlife viewing. January to March is excellent in the southern Serengeti for calving, and the Mara River crossings usually happen between July and October. The long rains in April and May are quieter and cheaper.

faqs.question: How many days do I need for a safari?
faqs.answer: Four to seven days lets you see two or three parks without rushing. Shorter trips of one to three days are possible from Arusha, and longer safaris allow more time in the Serengeti or a mix of north and south.

faqs.question: Are your safaris private or shared?
faqs.answer: Both. Private safaris are planned around your dates and pace. Joining safaris have fixed departures and a shared vehicle, which lowers the price per person.

faqs.question: What is included in the price?
faqs.answer: Each package page lists what is included, such as accommodation, meals as stated, park fees, a driver-guide and the vehicle, and what is not, such as international flights, visas, insurance and tips. Please check the list for the package you choose.

faqs.question: Do I need a visa to visit Tanzania?
faqs.answer: Most visitors need a visa, which can usually be arranged online in advance or on arrival, depending on your nationality. Rules change, so check the official immigration website before you travel. Your passport should be valid for at least six months.

faqs.question: Which vaccinations and health precautions do I need?
faqs.answer: Speak to a travel doctor well before you go. Malaria prevention is generally recommended, and a yellow fever certificate may be needed depending on where you have travelled. Carry travel insurance that covers medical evacuation.

faqs.question: How do I book and pay?
faqs.answer: Send a booking request on our website and we will reply with a quote and itinerary. A deposit confirms the booking and the balance is due before travel. We will confirm the payment methods and dates in your quote.

faqs.question: Can I change or cancel my booking?
faqs.answer: Our cancellation terms depend on how close to departure you cancel and on supplier policies. They are set out in your booking confirmation, and we recommend travel insurance that covers cancellation.

faqs.question: Can you adjust an itinerary?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private itineraries can be changed to suit your dates, interests, budget and accommodation level. Tell us what you would like and we will adjust the plan and price.

faqs.question: How fit do I need to be to climb Kilimanjaro?
faqs.answer: You need good general fitness and the willingness to walk for several hours a day for multiple days. No technical climbing is needed. Training with hill walks in the months before helps, and a longer route gives a better chance of reaching the summit.

faqs.question: What is the best route on Kilimanjaro?
faqs.answer: Longer routes such as Lemosho, Machame (seven days) and the Northern Circuit give better acclimatisation. Marangu is the only route with huts, and Rongai suits the wetter months. We can help you pick one based on your experience and dates.

faqs.question: What is the best time to climb Kilimanjaro?
faqs.answer: The main seasons are January to March and June to October, when conditions are generally drier. Weather on the mountain can change quickly in any month.

faqs.question: What should I pack for a safari?
faqs.answer: Light neutral clothing, a warm layer for early mornings, a hat, sunglasses, sun protection, insect repellent, binoculars, a camera, comfortable shoes and personal medication. Soft bags are easier to load than hard suitcases.

faqs.question: Is it safe to travel in Tanzania?
faqs.answer: Tanzania is generally welcoming and most trips pass without trouble. Take normal precautions in towns, follow your guide's wildlife instructions and check current travel advice for your country before you go.

faqs.question: Do you offer Zanzibar beach extensions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many guests finish a safari with a few days on Zanzibar, and we can arrange flights, hotels and transfers as part of your package.
